summary.text: An 85-year-old man with prior 45 pack-year smoking exposure, CAD with three-vessel CABG, diabetes, hypertension and CKD presented with progressive abdominal pain, diarrhea and chest pressure. A renal ultrasound five years earlier showed moderate right RAS with PSV 168 cm/s. Admission BP 247/120 mmHg, HR 126 and AKI/eosinophilia accompanied troponin T 314→388 ng/L at six hours and EKG abnormalities. ACS and aortic dissection were considered then ruled out. Noncontrast CT showed marked aortic/proximal renal arterial calcification. The conflicting body/caption historical creatinine ranges remain unresolved.

Initial IV labetalol 20 mg and hydralazine 20 mg every 4 hours improved BP to 129/54 and resolved chest pressure. Diarrhea improved, but serum creatinine rose to 4.1 and BP rebounded to 188/81 despite home-antihypertensive uptitration. Echo showed generalized hypokinesis, LVEF 37%, estimated RVSP 51 mmHg and an enlarged IVC with normal collapse. Doppler showed left renal atrophy and severe right RAS/PSV 397 cm/s. Acute decompensated heart failure/flash pulmonary edema required ICU transfer, BiPAP and clevidipine/furosemide infusion support.

Selective right angiography confirmed a critical calcified ostial lesion. IV heparin and wire crossing preceded sequential balloon dilation with persistent narrowing, then a 5×15 mm Herculink right stent expanded to 5.5 mm produced a patent lumen/brisk flow without distal embolization. Subsequent critical left ostial stenosis could not be crossed; no further left intervention was pursued because of advanced atrophy. Angio-Seal achieved hemostasis and no complications were reported. Postprocedural aspirin 81 mg/clopidogrel 75 mg dual therapy preceded clinical resolution over following days. Caption-only immediate creatinine 3.9 mg/dL downtrended to baseline by discharge; short-term outpatient creatinine was 1.5 mg/dL. No exact calendar date/long-term interval supplied. Suspected atheroembolism and proposed mechanisms remain qualified.

evidence.quote: In our case, AKI was multifactorial. Prolonged diarrhea triggered hypovolemia, reducing effective intravascular volume and renal perfusion. This prerenal insult was particularly significant given the patient’s severe right renal artery stenosis and atrophic left kidney, rendering him functionally uninephric. In addition, marked eosinophilia raised concern for renal atheroembolism, possibly precipitated by hemodynamic instability or prior arterial manipulation. Superimposed on this, the patient’s hypertensive emergency reflected activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) in response to renal hypoperfusion. Severe hypertension not only worsened renal injury directly, but also precipitated acute cardiac dysfunction with pulmonary edema. The resulting renal venous congestion and possible low cardiac output further aggravated kidney injury, exemplifying the bidirectional interaction of the heart and kidney in the setting of RAS. The temporal resolution of renal dysfunction and hemodynamic instability following stenting strongly suggests that revascularization played a causal role in reversing this downward spiral. Importantly, minimal parenchymal disease in the right kidney and the absence of proteinuria favored a successful outcome after PTRAS. ^(,)

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 3
The trend of creatinine over time is depicted above. The baseline level was 1.6-9 mg/dL, with an increase to 2.2 mg/dL on admission. At the time of ICU transfer, creatinine peaked at 4.1 mg/dL. Immediately after percutaneous right renal artery stenting, creatinine remained stable at 3.9 mg/dL. However, it subsequently quickly downtrended to baseline at discharge and was 1.5 mg/dL at short-term outpatient follow-up.

article_limitations: One original index patient. Literature/cohort thresholds and medication recommendations are background, not delivered patient therapies. No dialysis, measured RAAS, translesional pressure gradient, drug dose/route beyond source, fixed renal-stent stenosis percentage, calendar dates or long-term follow-up inferred.

Baseline body/caption creatinine conflict is retained review-only. Immediate post-stent 3.9 and short-term follow-up 1.5 are caption/text respectively; the chart discharge point is separately inspected pixel evidence.

Left intervention did not proceed after failed crossing; right wire/balloon/stent and closure are distinct supported stages. Atheroembolism remains a differential. Caption-grounded clinical image companion and actually inspected pixels remain separate.
